title: The EHR goes dark at 02:10

injects.title: 02:10 The EHR stops
injects.text: Every unit reports the EHR frozen at sign-in. The hosting team cannot give a time to restore. Night census: 214 inpatients and 19 patients in the emergency department.

injects.title: 02:50 A new patient, no chart
injects.text: The emergency department receives an unconscious man from a road crash with no identification. Registration cannot open the EHR to create a record, and blood must go to the lab now.

injects.title: 04:00 A critical result with nowhere to go
injects.text: The lab analyzers run, but results cannot reach the EHR. A critical result comes off the analyzer for a patient on 3 West.

injects.title: 06:30 The EHR is back
injects.text: The hosting team restores the EHR. Four hours of paper orders, notes, medication records and results sit on every unit, and the trauma patient now has a name.

objective: EHR safety practices: reliable patient identification, planning for downtime and closing the loop on test results
secondaryObjectives: Usability and safety as properties of the whole socio-technical system, and unintended consequences such as workarounds
The socio-technical view: people and organizations as the ultimate users of health information technology

sources.cite: ONC/ASTP, SAFER Guides, Contingency Planning (SAFER Self Assessment, August 2024; the SAFER Guides page lists the 2025 guides, updated February 27, 2026)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of the PDF linked from healthit.gov/safer. 1.3: 'Paper forms are available to replace key EHR functions during downtimes', enough in each patient care area for at least 8 hours, with 'a process in place to ensure that the information recorded on paper during the downtime gets entered and reconciled into the EHR'. 1.4: a 'read-only' backup EHR 'updated frequently (optimally at least hourly)'. 1.5: register new patients during downtime with 'unique temporary patient record numbers' and reconcile them when the EHR returns. 2.1: unannounced downtime drills at least once a year. 2.2: notify staff by methods 'other than those that rely on the same computing infrastructure as the EHR', and when it is back. 2.3: a written downtime policy saying 'when a downtime should be called' and 'who will be in charge', with a paper copy on the units. 2.5: 'Ensure that all system interface buffers are empty prior to stopping or restarting the system.' The guide has no standalone results practice; the case's read-back of critical results is the author's reading of closing the loop (the Test Results SAFER guide, not read for this round).

Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: eight 2025 guides (High Priority Practices, Organizational Responsibilities, Contingency Planning, System Management, Patient Identification, CPOE with Decision Support, Test Results Reporting and Follow-Up, Clinician Communication); Contingency Planning 'identifies recommended safety practices associated with planned or unplanned EHR unavailability'.

sources.cite: AMIA Accreditation Committee, foundational domains for master's-level health informatics education (CAHIIM HI master's curriculum requirements PDF)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. F5 (Human Factors and Socio-technical Systems) examines how human behaviors and information technologies interact, with 'consideration and respect for the role of users in the design and application' of systems.

Riverbend Medical Center (fictional), its census, times and gaps are invented teaching values. The case is an exercise at the level of process: it names no drug, dose, test value or patient, and gives no clinical instruction.

brief.situation: You are the clinical informatics specialist on call at Riverbend Medical Center (fictional), and tonight's tabletop exercise has you coordinate an unplanned EHR downtime. The facilitator reads the scenario in injects from 02:10. The house supervisor, the emergency department, the lab, the EHR team and health information management are at the table.
handover: The downtime policy says the house supervisor and the informatics on call call a downtime together. Each unit has a downtime box with paper forms and registration packets, and two downtime workstations show a read-only backup of the EHR.
Email and the intranet run on the same infrastructure as the EHR tonight.
howItWorks: The clock is scenario time: each decision or question to the table takes minutes, and the facilitator's next inject arrives on the same clock.
The table shows the injects, who is engaged, the communications and the decision log. A role marked 'gap' is something the plan does not cover.
When you call the end of the exercise you write the after-action report and explain your reasoning.

source.note: The facilitator ends the scenario at 08:10.

writeup.question: For the hot wash: what kept patients safe tonight, what nearly did not, and what changes before the next downtime?

parts.label: The safety practices
parts.criteria: Downtime called early by the people the policy names; staff told by a channel that does not run on the EHR's infrastructure; unique temporary record numbers for new patients; critical results phoned with read-back and logged (closing the loop); interfaces restarted after the queues drained, with back-entry and reconciliation of records and numbers.
parts.modelAnswer: Called at once, paged and texted, downtime numbers, phoned results with read-back, drained queues then back-entry and merge.

parts.label: The workarounds
parts.criteria: Names the socio-technical risk: scrap paper, 'Doe' names, results in trays and filed paper are workarounds that move risk rather than remove it.
parts.modelAnswer: Every workaround tonight would have broken identification or the result loop.

parts.label: The improvement plan
parts.criteria: The gaps found (two hours of forms against at least eight, a backup 26 hours stale against at least hourly, no clear lead and no paper policy on the unit) each get an owner and a date; drills at least yearly.
parts.modelAnswer: Forms restock owner and date; backup refresh monitored hourly; policy on paper with the named leads; an unannounced drill this year.

expertPath.text: Call the downtime with the house supervisor; overhead page and text to every unit; brief the administrator on call.
Unique downtime record number for the unidentified patient; ask how current the backup is and how many hours of forms the units hold.
Critical results phoned with read-back and logged on both ends; ask who is in charge and where the paper policy is.
Restart interfaces once their queues drain; announce it; back-entry and the record merge by HIM.

exercised.headline: Good: safe through the dark
exercised.body: The downtime was called at once and heard on every unit, the new patient was uniquely identified, results closed the loop by read-back, and the record came back whole. The exercise found three gaps and gave each an owner.

partly.headline: Partly tested
partly.body: Patients were kept safe in the scenario, but a call came late, the staff message went by a channel that was down, or a gap was missed or left without an owner.

wrongPatient.headline: Identification failed
wrongPatient.body: Shared placeholder names are how samples reach the wrong patient. Downtime registration packets exist to give every new patient a unique number from the first minute.

lostResult.headline: The result loop was open
lostResult.body: A result is closed when the responsible clinician has acknowledged it, not when it is printed. Phone critical results with read-back and log both ends.

lostRecord.headline: The record was left with a hole
lostRecord.body: Coming back up is part of the downtime: drain the interface queues before restarting, back-enter the paper and merge temporary numbers into the real record.

noReport.headline: No after-action
noReport.body: An exercise is for finding gaps. Without an owner and a date, none of them closes.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No after-action report was written before the case's limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: An EHR downtime is a socio-technical event: the system fails, and the safety of patients depends on what people do instead. Call it at once, through the people the policy names, and tell staff by a channel that does not share the EHR's infrastructure. Give every new patient a unique temporary record number so identification never rests on a placeholder name. Close the loop on critical results with a phone call, read-back and a log at both ends. When the EHR returns, drain interface queues before restarting, then back-enter paper records and merge temporary numbers. The exercise's job is to find gaps: forms for two hours against the guide's eight, a backup a day stale against hourly, and no clear lead or paper policy; each needs an owner and a date.
